title: Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator
description: Four fixed challenges ask the learner to calculate air velocity, airflow or minimum flow area for rectangular and round ducts using Q = V x A, checked within 2 percent with step-by-step feedback; Explore mode then shows how velocity changes with duct size at fixed CFM.
creator: Twin City Fan

Air velocity

educational.audience: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff
educational.topic: Airflow, velocity and flow area in ducts (Q = V x A)
learningObjectives: The learner will calculate air velocity, airflow volume or required flow area from the other two quantities for rectangular and round ducts, to within 2 percent of the model value.
prerequisites: Airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
Air velocity in feet per minute
The equation Q = V x A
Converting duct dimensions in inches to square feet

accessibility.notes: describe() text (fallback mode); verdicts, the Explore-mode note and the mastery line announced through FP.announce (aria-live); ✓/✗ glyphs and solid/dashed feedback borders pair with colour; the departure step is marked with ▶ and an outline; Enter checks and goes to the next challenge; every control is a native, focusable p5 control.

equations: Round A = pi x D^2 / 576 ft^2
rules: Two attempts per challenge; non-numeric or empty input does not use an attempt
Challenge model values rounded to 1 ft/min, 1 CFM and 0.01 ft^2; Explore-mode velocity shown to the nearest 10 ft/min
Mastery: 4 of 4 correct, at most two attempts each
assumptions: Velocity is the average velocity over the full duct cross-section
Duct dimensions are inside dimensions in inches
limitations: Every dimension is at least 6 in, so area is never zero

sources: Challenge 1: the chapter's machine-shop worked example (Chapter 1, Air Velocity)

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Committed-answer practice problems with immediate diagnostic feedback, followed by Explore mode
keyQuestions: Why must duct dimensions in inches be divided by 144 before dividing CFM by area?
Does a bigger duct move more air when the fan airflow is unchanged?
Is a round duct of diameter D the same area as a square duct of side D?
commonMisconceptions: Velocity can be found by dividing CFM by the duct dimensions in inches without converting to square feet.
A bigger duct moves more air at the same fan airflow; in fact the CFM is the same and only the velocity drops.
A round duct of diameter D has the same area as a square duct of side D.
assessmentOpportunities: Running score shown as 'Challenges correct: n of 4'; mastery is 4 of 4 correct within 2 percent, at most two attempts each.
Explore mode is not evidence of mastery
